question: v10
q: How's the job market looking for women in Victoria?

transcript.answer:
**The job market for women in Victoria has weakened noticeably over the past year, and it's softer than for women nationally.** The latest data is for September 2026 (ABS Labour Force, seasonally adjusted, women only).

**Main figures, September 2026 vs August 2025**

| Measure | Victoria Sep 2026 | Victoria Aug 2025 | Australia Sep 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unemployment rate | **5.1%** | 4.0% | 4.6% |
| Participation rate | 63.6% | 63.8% | 63.1% |
| Share of women employed | 60.4% | 61.3% | 60.2% |
| Women employed | 1.843m | 1.833m | 7.103m |
| Full-time | 1.008m | 1.016m | 4.107m |

**What stands out**

- **Unemployment is up about 1 point in a year.** It went from 4.0% (Aug 2025) to 5.1%, and was 4.0–4.1% as late as January 2026. It jumped in March–April (4.7% in April), dipped in May, then rose above 5% from June. It peaked at 5.2% in July and has eased slightly since (5.16% in August, 5.10% in September), but it's still high.
- **It's worse than the national rate.** A year ago, Victorian women had about the same unemployment rate as women nationally (both around 4.0–4.1%). Now Victoria is about 0.5 points higher (5.1% vs 4.6%).
- **Few new jobs.** About 9,600 more women are employed than a year ago (+0.5%), less than population growth. That's why the share of women in work fell by 0.9 points. Employment hit a low in April 2026 (1.803m) and has since recovered to last year's level, but not much higher.
- **The jobs have shifted towards part-time work.** Full-time employment fell by about 7,500 over the year. By my calculation (total minus full-time), part-time work rose by about 17,000, to roughly 835,000. Nationally it's the opposite: full-time jobs for women grew strongly (+108,000) while part-time fell.
- **Women haven't stopped looking for work.** Participation is about the same as a year ago (63.6%) and has come back from its April low of 62.4%. So the higher unemployment mostly reflects more women job-hunting than there are jobs, not women leaving the workforce.

**Bottom line:** Women in Victoria are still looking for work at about the same rate, but unemployment has risen to around 5%, its highest in this period. New jobs have mostly been part-time, and conditions are softer than for women nationally. Unemployment has stopped rising since July, but there isn't a clear recovery yet. Monthly state-level figures for one sex are fairly volatile, so the trend matters more than any single month.
